text: A rocket [[@rocket-fuel|burns fuel]] to make a huge amount of hot gas, then forces that gas out of a nozzle at the bottom at enormous speed. As the gas shoots down, the rocket is pushed up. This push is called [[thrust|thrust]].

It works because of a rule discovered by [[@newton-life|Isaac Newton]]: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. Stand on a skateboard and throw a heavy ball forward, and you roll backward. A rocket does the same thing, throwing out tonnes of gas every second.
Unlike a jet engine, a rocket carries its own oxygen, or another chemical that does the same job. That means it can keep burning fuel in space, where there is no air.

st.prompt: Space has no air. How can a rocket keep speeding up out there?

options.t: Throwing gas out of the back pushes the rocket forward
It pushes against leftover air
The pull of other planets drags it along

st.reveal: When a rocket blasts gas backwards, the gas pushes the rocket forwards with an equal force. It doesn't need anything to push against. In fact rockets work slightly better in empty space than in air.

myth: Rockets fly by pushing against the air, so they can't work in space.

Rockets push against their own exhaust, not the air. In 1920 a New York Times editorial wrongly mocked Robert Goddard for saying rockets could work in a vacuum. In July 1969, as Apollo 11 flew to the Moon, the paper printed a correction.

sec.t:
Getting into orbit is hard. To circle Earth without falling back, a spacecraft needs to travel sideways at about 28,000 km/h. To reach that speed, a rocket needs vast amounts of fuel, so most of a rocket's weight on the launch pad is fuel. Often it is around 90 per cent.

To save weight, big rockets are built in stages, stacked on top of each other. When the bottom stage runs out of fuel, it drops away and the next stage fires. The rocket keeps getting lighter, so it can go faster. India's [[@isro-launch|LVM3]], which carried [[@chandrayaan|Chandrayaan-3]] towards the Moon in 2023, has three stages.

sec.h: From fire arrows to the Moon
sec.t:
Rockets are old. People in China were using gunpowder rockets by the 1200s, related to the [[@fireworks|fireworks]] we still enjoy. In the late 1700s, the armies of Hyder Ali and [[@tipu-sultan|Tipu Sultan]] of Mysore fired rockets with iron casings at British troops. The British studied captured ones and used them to design their own war rockets.

Modern rockets began with the American scientist Robert Goddard. On 16 March 1926, in a snowy field in Massachusetts, he launched the first rocket powered by liquid fuel. It flew for about 2.5 seconds and reached about 12 m high, roughly the height of a four-storey building. Less than 45 years later, a far bigger liquid-fuel rocket, the Saturn V, sent astronauts to the Moon.

sec.h: A church, a bicycle and a rocket

sec.t:
A rocket on the launch pad is steered by swivelling its engine nozzles, a bit like pointing a hose. Once in space, spacecraft use small thrusters to turn and adjust their path.

Rockets are also getting [[@reusable-rockets|reusable]]. Since 2015, SpaceX has landed the first stages of its Falcon 9 rockets upright, then flown them again, sometimes more than 20 times. ISRO is testing a reusable winged vehicle called Pushpak. For most of history a rocket was used once and thrown away. That is starting to change.

text: Sputnik 1 was the first artificial satellite, the first object made by humans to go into orbit around Earth. The Soviet Union launched it on 4 October 1957. It was a shiny aluminium ball about 58 cm wide, a bit smaller than a beach ball, with four long thin antennas trailing behind.

Sputnik did one simple thing. It sent out radio beeps as it raced around Earth every 96 minutes. That was enough to amaze and alarm the world. It started the space age, and with it a contest between the Soviet Union and the United States known as the [[@space-race|space race]].

st.prompt: Sputnik carried no cameras and no scientists. How did people around the world know it was really up there?

options.t: Anyone with a good radio could hear it beeping
It sent back photos of Earth
It flashed a bright light in Morse code

st.reveal: Sputnik broadcast a steady "beep, beep, beep" on radio frequencies that amateur radio fans could pick up. People taped the sound, and radio stations played it. It was impossible to fake.

d.try: With a friend in another room or across the garden, make up a simple code using a torch or a whistle, such as one beep for yes and two for no. Send each other messages. Sputnik's beeps were a little like this, and scientists even learned about the upper air from how its signal changed.
myth: The bright dot people watched crossing the sky in 1957 was Sputnik itself.
Sputnik was small and hard to see with bare eyes. The bright moving light most people saw was the rocket's large core stage, which was also in orbit, about 26 m long and much more reflective.

sec.t:
"Sputnik" is a Russian word meaning "fellow traveller" or "companion". The satellite weighed about 84 kg, about as much as a grown man. Inside its sealed ball were batteries, two radio transmitters and a fan to keep them cool.

It was launched from a secret site in the desert of Kazakhstan, now called the [[@launch-sites|Baikonur Cosmodrome]], on top of an R-7 rocket. The R-7 had been designed to carry nuclear weapons across the world. The engineer in charge, Sergei Korolev, was so secret that the Soviet public didn't know his name until after he died in 1966.

Sputnik's beeps used [[@radio-waves|radio waves]] at frequencies that radio hobbyists everywhere could tune into. Within hours, people in many countries were listening. Newspapers printed times when it would pass overhead.

{{story:radio-waves}}

The batteries ran out after 21 days, and the beeping stopped. Sputnik kept circling silently. Each orbit, the thin outer air dragged on it a tiny bit. On 4 January 1958, after about 1,400 orbits, it dropped low enough to burn up like a shooting star.

Scientists still learned from it. By tracking how its orbit shrank, they measured how dense the air is high above Earth. By studying how the radio signal changed, they learned about the electrically charged layer of the atmosphere.

In the United States, Sputnik caused something close to panic. This was the [[@cold-war|Cold War]], a long rivalry between the two countries. Americans worried that a country able to put a satellite in orbit could also send a rocket across the world.

The US responded fast. Its first attempt to launch a satellite, in December 1957, exploded on the launch pad. On 31 January 1958, it succeeded with Explorer 1, which discovered belts of radiation circling Earth, now called the Van Allen belts. In October 1958, the US set up a new space agency, NASA. It also spent much more on science and maths education in schools.

Just a month after Sputnik 1, on 3 November 1957, Sputnik 2 carried the [[@space-animals|first animal]] into orbit, a [[@dogs-domestic|stray dog]] from Moscow named Laika. Her spacecraft was never designed to return, and she died within hours, probably because the cabin overheated. Her flight showed that a living creature could survive launch and float in orbit, but it is still remembered with sadness.

Less than four years after Sputnik 1, the Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the [[@first-in-space|first person in space]].

In 1957 there was one working satellite. Today there are more than 10,000. They forecast weather, beam television, guide ships and phones, and photograph every corner of Earth.

India joined in 1975, when the Soviet Union launched [[@space-aryabhata-satellite|India's first satellite]], [[@aryabhata|Aryabhata]]. Five years later, India launched a satellite on its own rocket for the first time. All of them trace their story back to a beeping ball that went round the world in an hour and a half.

text: Homing pigeons are a tame breed of the rock dove, the same species as the pigeons in city squares. People have bred them for thousands of years for one unusual skill: finding their way back to their home loft from places they have never been.

Scientists still don't fully understand how they do it. Experiments suggest pigeons use several senses together. They use the Sun as a compass, and they can sense Earth's magnetic field. Smells carried on the wind seem to help them work out where they are. Close to home, they recognise landmarks like rivers, roads and buildings.
A homing pigeon can fly hundreds of kilometres in a day and find its own roof at the end.

options.t: They flew off in the wrong direction
They flew home perfectly

st.reveal: Pigeons use the Sun as a compass, but the Sun moves across the sky during the day. To use it, they need to know the time. With their clocks shifted, they misjudged the Sun's position and set off at a large angle from the right direction. On cloudy days, they used other senses.

sec.t:
The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west, but its position changes all day. To use it as a compass, a pigeon must know the time. Pigeons have a good internal [[@jet-lag|body clock]].

In experiments, scientists shifted pigeons' clocks by keeping them under lights that switched on and off at the wrong times. On sunny days, these birds flew off in the wrong direction, just as you would expect if they were reading the Sun with a wrong clock.

On cloudy days, though, the same pigeons still got home. So they must have a backup.

In the 1970s, the American scientist William Keeton glued small magnets to pigeons' heads. On sunny days, they homed normally. On cloudy days, many got lost. This suggested they sense [[@earth-magnet|Earth's magnetic field]] when the Sun is hidden. How they detect it is still debated. Iron-rich cells in pigeons' beaks were once thought to be the sensor, but later studies found they were mostly immune cells.

Italian scientists found that pigeons whose sense of smell was blocked often struggled to home from unfamiliar places. They suggested pigeons learn a "smell map" from the winds blowing over their loft. Not all scientists are convinced, and it may matter more in some places than others.

Close to home, pigeons use what they see. In the early 2000s, a team at the University of Oxford fitted pigeons with tiny GPS trackers. Many birds followed main roads and motorways, even turning at roundabouts, rather than flying in a straight line.

{{story:world-war-one}}

Before radio, pigeons carried urgent messages. In the [[@world-war-one|First World War]], armies kept thousands of them. In October 1918, an American battalion was trapped in a forest in France, and shells from its own side were falling on it. A pigeon named Cher Ami flew through gunfire with a note giving their position. The bird arrived badly wounded, but the shelling stopped and about 190 soldiers survived. Cher Ami was long thought to be female, until a DNA test in 2021 showed he was male. His preserved body is at the [[@smithsonian|Smithsonian museum]] in Washington, DC.

In the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], Britain gave a special medal for animal bravery, the Dickin Medal. Between 1943 and 1949, pigeons won 32 of them, more than any other kind of animal in those years.

sec.h: Pigeon post in India and beyond
sec.t:
In 1850, before the [[@telegraph|telegraph]] linked the two cities, Paul Julius Reuter used pigeons to carry [[@stock-market|stock market]] news between Aachen in Germany and Brussels in Belgium. His news business later became the famous Reuters agency.

In India, the [[@odisha|Odisha]] Police ran a pigeon service from about 1946. The birds carried messages from remote areas, and during floods when other links failed. It was one of the last police pigeon services in the world when it was closed around 2008, as mobile phones spread.

Today, pigeon racing is a popular sport from Kolkata to New York. Fanciers train their birds by releasing them further and further away. The best racers sell for huge sums: in 2020, a Belgian pigeon named New Kim sold at auction for €1.6 million.

text: A starfish eats in a way that sounds impossible. Its mouth is on its underside, in the middle. When it finds a mussel, clam or oyster, it wraps its arms around the shell and grips it with hundreds of tiny tube feet. Then it pulls, slowly and steadily, sometimes for hours. The shellfish eventually tires and its shell opens a crack.

That is all the starfish needs. It pushes part of its stomach out through its mouth and slides it into the gap. The stomach releases juices that start digesting the soft animal inside its own shell. When the meal has turned to soup, the starfish draws its stomach back in. Your own stomach works very differently, as you can read in [[@stomach-digest|how digestion works]].

st.reveal: The starfish grips the shell with hundreds of tube feet and pulls for a long time until the mussel tires. A gap less than a millimetre wide is enough. It slides part of its stomach through the gap and digests the mussel inside its own shell.

myth: Starfish are fish.

Starfish are not fish at all. They have no backbone, gills or fins. They belong to a group called echinoderms, along with sea urchins and sea cucumbers, which is why many scientists prefer the name sea star.

sec.t:
Turn a starfish over and you will see rows of small, soft tubes along each arm. These are tube feet. Each one is a little hollow tube, often with a sucker at its tip. The starfish moves them using water pumped through a network of canals inside its body, like a hydraulic machine.

By pumping water in and out, the starfish can stretch and pull back each foot. Hundreds of them working together let it crawl over rocks, cling on in crashing waves and pull open shells. Starfish have no [[@blood|blood]]. Seawater flowing through these canals does much of the work that blood does in other animals.

A starfish has no brain. Instead, a ring of nerves circles its mouth, with a nerve running down each arm. Each arm can sense and react, and somehow they work together, though scientists are still studying how.

Most starfish have five arms, arranged in a star pattern. That fivefold [[@symmetry|symmetry]] is shared with their relatives, the sea urchins and sand dollars. They belong to a group called [[echinoderm|echinoderms]], meaning "spiny skin". Some starfish have many more arms. The sunflower sea star of the Pacific coast of North America can have more than 20.

Many starfish can [[@power-axolotl|regrow a lost arm]]. In a few kinds, a single arm with part of the central body can grow into a whole new starfish.

{{story:stomach-digest}}

In the 1960s, an American scientist named Robert Paine did a simple experiment on the rocky coast of Washington State. In one area, he kept removing a purple starfish that ate mussels. In a nearby area, he left the starfish alone.

Without the starfish, mussels took over the rocks and crowded out many other animals and seaweeds. The variety of life dropped sharply. Paine called the starfish a [[keystone-species|keystone species]], after the central stone that holds up an arch. Take it away and the arch collapses. The idea is now used around the world to understand how nature fits together. You can see starfish like these in [[@tide-pools|tide pools]].

Since 2013, a disease called sea star wasting has killed billions of starfish along the Pacific coast of North America. Affected animals develop sores and fall apart within days. The sunflower sea star was among the worst hit, with its numbers crashing by more than 90 per cent across much of its range.

Sunflower sea stars eat sea urchins. Without them, urchins multiplied and munched through underwater forests of giant seaweed, as you can read in [[@kelp-forests|kelp forests]]. On the [[@great-barrier-reef|Great Barrier Reef]], the problem is reversed: outbreaks of the crown-of-thorns starfish eat large areas of coral.

text: When an axolotl loses a leg, the stump does not scar over the way your skin does. Instead, cells near the wound go back to an early, flexible state, a bit like they were in an embryo. They pile up into a little bump called a blastema. Over a few weeks, that bump grows into a brand-new leg, with bones, muscles, nerves and skin in all the right places.
Axolotls can do this for their tail, parts of their spinal cord, and even bits of their heart, eyes and brain. Scientists study them hoping to learn how human bodies might one day heal better.

st.reveal: The axolotl is a salamander that stays in its baby form, with feathery gills, its whole life. It breathes through gills, skin and simple lungs.

sec.h: A salamander that never grows up
sec.t:
The axolotl (say "AX-uh-lot-ul") is a salamander from the lakes around [[@mexico|Mexico City]]. Most salamanders start life in water with gills, then change into land animals, like tadpoles turning into [[@frogs-world|frogs]]. The axolotl skips that change. It keeps its frilly pink gills, which stick out of its head like a feathery crown, for its whole life.

Its face seems to be smiling. That, plus its pink, gold or dark colours, has made it a pet-shop favourite. The axolotl even appears on Mexico's 50-peso banknote.

Your body is built from [[@body-cells|cells]], and most of yours have fixed jobs: skin cells stay skin, bone cells stay bone. An axolotl's wound cells can partly forget their jobs. Skin cells, muscle cells and others near the cut become young again and start dividing quickly.

Nerves are essential. If the nerves to a limb are cut, the stump will not regrow. Somehow the nerve endings send signals that tell the blastema to keep building. The cells also seem to remember where they are, so a cut at the elbow grows a forearm and hand, not a whole new shoulder.

The new limb is not a rough copy. It works as well as the old one.

{{story:genes-family}}

In 2018, scientists finished reading the axolotl's genome, its full set of genetic instructions. It turned out to be about 32 billion letters long, roughly ten times the length of the human genome. Printed in ordinary books, it would fill a library.

Researchers are now hunting through it for the genes that switch regrowth on. Some of the same genes exist in people, but in us they seem to stay quiet after we are born.

A little. Your [[@liver|liver]] can regrow to near full size even if a large part is removed, which is why living people can donate part of theirs. Very young children can sometimes regrow the tip of a finger. Your skin and the lining of your gut replace themselves constantly. But a lost arm or leg does not come back.

Scientists hope that understanding axolotls might one day help wounds heal without scars, or help repair injured spinal cords. That is still a long way off.

sec.h: Millions in tanks, few in the wild
sec.t:
There is a sad twist. Axolotls are common in labs and aquariums around the world, yet in the wild they are Critically Endangered. They live naturally only in the canals of Xochimilco, the last remains of a great lake system the Aztecs once farmed. Surveys found about 6,000 axolotls per square kilometre in 1998, and only about 35 by 2014.

Pollution, a growing city, and introduced fish such as carp and tilapia, which eat axolotl eggs and young, are to blame. Local farmers and scientists are now cleaning some canals to make refuges. And the axolotl is not the only amphibian with a superpower: one North American frog can [[@power-wood-frog|freeze solid]] all winter and hop away in spring.

text: Emperor penguins breed in the middle of the Antarctic winter, on sea ice far from open water. The mother lays a single egg, then she is exhausted and hungry. So she passes the egg to the father and walks back to the sea to feed.

The father keeps the egg warm on top of his feet, under a fold of feathery skin called a brood pouch. For about 65 days, through months of darkness, he hardly moves and eats nothing. Only when the mother returns, around the time the chick hatches, can he finally head off to eat. By then he may have fasted for about four months.

myth: Penguins live at both the North Pole and the South Pole.
Wild penguins live almost entirely in the Southern Hemisphere. There are none in the Arctic. Polar bears and penguins only meet in cartoons and zoos.

sec.t:
It sounds like a terrible plan. Temperatures can drop below -40°C and storms can blow at well over 100 km/h. But timing is everything. A chick needs months to grow its waterproof feathers. If eggs hatch in late winter, chicks are ready to swim by summer, when the sea ice breaks up and food is plentiful.

The mother has already used much of her energy to make the egg. Sending her back to the ocean first means someone is always building up strength for the next stage.

The fathers survive by huddling. Thousands of birds press together, often about 10 to every square metre. The middle of a huddle can rise above 30°C, so hot that birds sometimes have to step out to cool down.

Nobody gets stuck on the cold edge forever. Every so often the whole huddle shuffles a few centimetres. These small moves ripple through the crowd like a wave, slowly rotating birds between the centre and the outside, each still carrying an egg on his feet.

During the fast, a father can lose up to about 40% of his body weight. If the chick hatches before the mother is back, he does something strange. He makes a thick, milky, protein-rich food in his oesophagus, the tube to his stomach, and feeds it to the chick. It can keep the chick going for a few days.

When the mother returns, she finds her partner by his call, among thousands of other penguins. Each bird's voice is different. Then they swap, and the thin dad finally heads for the sea.

sec.h: A terrible journey for three eggs
sec.t: In July 1911, three men from Robert Falcon Scott's British expedition walked through the polar night to an emperor colony at Cape Crozier. They wanted eggs to study how birds evolved. Temperatures fell to about -60°C. One of them, Apsley Cherry-Garrard, later called his book about it The Worst Journey in the World. The tale is part of the bigger story of [[@explorers-poles|polar explorers]].

Today scientists find emperor colonies using satellites, by spotting the brown stains of penguin droppings on white ice. A count from 2009 found about 595,000 adults. In 2022, sea ice broke up early in one region and thousands of chicks were lost before they could swim. A 2025 study found that emperor numbers in one large region had fallen by about a fifth since 2009. The link between disappearing sea ice and a warming planet is explained in [[@climate-change|climate change]].

In 2006 the film March of the Penguins, which follows this winter march, won an [[@oscars|Oscar]] in the USA.

text: Thread is weak on its own. To make cloth, you have to lock lots of it together. There are two main ways.

Weaving uses two sets of threads at right angles. The long threads, called the warp, are stretched tight on a frame called a [[loom|loom]]. A second thread, the weft, goes over and under them from side to side, row after row. Knitting uses just one long yarn. It is pulled through itself in rows of loops, each row hanging from the one before.
Woven cloth is firm and holds its shape. Knitted cloth stretches, because the loops can open and close. That is why socks and sweaters are knitted, and shirts and jeans are woven.

myth: Knitting is as old as weaving.

Weaving goes back many thousands of years. The oldest true knitting found so far is about a thousand years old, from Egypt. Some older pieces that look knitted were made by a different looping method using a single needle.

sec.t:
The simplest weave goes over one warp thread and under the next, then does the opposite on the next row. That gives plain weave, used in cotton shirts and the khadi that Indians spun and wove by hand during the freedom movement.

Change the pattern and you change the cloth. In a twill weave, each row shifts one step sideways, making diagonal lines. Look closely at your jeans and you will see them. Denim is a twill with blue warp threads and white weft threads, which is why the inside of your jeans is paler than the outside. In satin weave, threads float over several others at once, which makes the surface shiny and smooth.

A loom makes the over-and-under quicker. Pedals lift every other warp thread at once, leaving a gap called a shed. A shuttle carrying the weft shoots through, the pedals swap, and the next row goes back the other way.

Knitting needs no loom, just two needles, or later a machine. Each stitch pulls a loop of yarn through a loop below it. Because the whole fabric can be one thread, a dropped stitch can run like a ladder down a sock.

In 1589, an English clergyman named William Lee built a frame that could knit stockings by machine. Queen Elizabeth I is said to have refused him a patent, worried it would put hand knitters out of work. Today, huge circular knitting machines make tubes of T-shirt fabric at high speed. Hundreds of needles sit in a ring, each one hooking a fresh loop as the ring spins, so the fabric grows downwards like a long sock.

India has woven cloth for at least 4,500 years. A scrap of cotton cloth was found at Mohenjo-daro, one of the cities of the Indus Valley. Today most cloth is made on power looms, but India still has about 35 lakh handloom workers, according to the 2019–20 government census. They weave Banarasi silk, Kanchipuram sarees and Assam's muga silk on looms in their homes.

Knitting has its own hubs. Ludhiana in Punjab is known for woollen sweaters, and Tiruppur in Tamil Nadu for cotton T-shirts. Weaving still rules in Kashmir, though. There, soft [[@wool|wool]] from mountain goats is spun and woven by hand into pashmina shawls, and some are embroidered for months afterwards.

text: A guitar makes sound when you pluck or strum its strings. Each string vibrates back and forth very fast. On an acoustic guitar, the strings pass their shaking to a thin wooden top, and the hollow body fills with vibrating air that comes out loud through the round sound hole.

To change the note, you press a string against a metal strip on the neck, called a fret. That shortens the part of the string that can vibrate. A shorter string vibrates faster and makes a higher note. An electric guitar works differently: it has a solid body and turns the strings' movement into an electric signal that an amplifier makes loud.

st.reveal: An electric guitar's pickups are magnets wrapped in fine wire. Only a vibrating metal string disturbs the magnetic field and creates a small electric signal. Nylon doesn't affect a magnet at all.

myth: An electric guitar has a tiny microphone inside that picks up the sound.
The pickups don't listen to sound at all. They are magnets with coils of wire, and they sense the movement of the steel strings directly. That is why an unplugged electric guitar sounds very quiet.

sec.h: Six strings and a lot of frets
sec.t:
Most guitars have six strings, tuned from low to high as E, A, D, G, B and E. The thickest string gives the deepest note. The thinnest gives the highest.

Frets are spaced closer together as they go up the neck. Each one raises the note by a semitone, the smallest step on a piano. The twelfth fret sits exactly halfway along the string. Pressing there halves the vibrating length and gives the same note one octave higher, the same rule a sitar player uses, as explained in [[@sitar-strings|high and low notes]].

sec.h: From lutes to the classical guitar
sec.t:
Instruments with a neck, a hollow body and plucked strings have existed for thousands of years. The lute and the Arabic oud are close relatives of the guitar.

In [[@spain|Spain]], during the 1800s, a craftsman named Antonio de Torres settled the shape of the modern classical guitar. He made the body larger and braced the wooden top with thin strips in a fan pattern, giving a richer sound. Classical guitars still use soft nylon strings. Guitars with steel strings, louder and brighter, became popular in the USA for folk, country and blues music.

In the 1920s and 1930s, guitarists in big dance bands had a problem. Trumpets and drums drowned them out. Inventors in the USA began fitting guitars with pickups. One of the first electric guitars sold, in the early 1930s, was a round, flat instrument nicknamed the "Frying Pan".

In the 1950s, solid-body electric guitars by companies such as Fender and Gibson became popular. They didn't howl with feedback as easily as hollow guitars, and they could be played very loud. They became the sound of [[@rock-music|rock and roll]].

sec.h: A Hawaiian twist and an Indian star
sec.t:
In [[@hawaii-islands|Hawaii]] in the late 1800s, players began laying the guitar flat on their lap and sliding a smooth steel bar along the strings. Notes could glide smoothly instead of jumping. This Hawaiian steel guitar spread around the world, as you can read in [[@hawaii-culture|Hawaiian culture]].

Indian musicians loved it, because sliding notes suit Indian music well. Vishwa Mohan Bhatt added extra strings to create the Mohan [[@veena|veena]], which he plays sitting cross-legged. In 1994, his album with the American guitarist Ry Cooder, *A Meeting by the River*, won a Grammy award. The guitar had come home in a new shape.

text: Khadi is cloth that is both spun into thread by hand and woven by hand. It's usually made from [[@clothes-cotton|cotton]], though silk and wool khadi exist too. Because every thread is spun on a wheel and woven on a handloom, no two lengths are exactly alike.

In the early 1900s, khadi became much more than cloth. Mahatma Gandhi asked Indians to spin their own thread and wear khadi instead of machine-made cloth from British mills. Spinning became a daily act of protest that anyone could join, rich or poor, young or old. The *charkha*, or spinning wheel, became a symbol of India's struggle for freedom.

st.prompt: Before India's flag had the Ashoka Chakra, what did the Congress party's flag from the freedom struggle have in its centre?

A lotus flower
A tiger

st.reveal: The flag adopted by the Indian National Congress in 1931 had a charkha in the middle. In 1947 it was replaced by the Ashoka Chakra, a wheel from Emperor Ashoka's lion pillar, for independent India's national flag.

d.try: Take a ball of cotton wool from a first-aid box. Pinch a little and pull it out gently while twisting it between your fingers. Keep pulling and twisting, and you'll see the loose fibres turn into a thin thread. This is the basic idea of spinning, the first step in making khadi.
myth: Khadi is just plain, rough, old-fashioned cloth.
Khadi can be coarse, but it can also be very fine, and it comes in many colours and weaves. Designers use it in modern clothes, and its loose weave lets air through, so it stays cool in summer.

sec.t:
For centuries India had been famous for its cotton, as you can read in [[@textiles-india|How did Indian cloth amaze the world?]]. Under British rule, raw cotton was shipped to factories in Britain, turned into cloth by machines, and sold back to India. Millions of Indian spinners and weavers lost their work.

Gandhi saw this as a trap. Every time an Indian bought foreign cloth, money left India and village workers stayed poor. If Indians made their own cloth, he argued, villages would earn again and the country would depend less on Britain. This idea of buying Indian goods was called *swadeshi*, "of one's own country".

From about 1920, khadi became the uniform of the freedom movement. Leaders, students and volunteers wore white khadi kurtas, dhotis and saris, and the khadi cap became a familiar sight. During the protests of the early 1920s, people made huge bonfires of foreign cloth in cities like Bombay.

Wearing khadi was a quiet but visible statement. A person in khadi was saying, without any words, that they supported [[@freedom-struggle|the freedom struggle]]. The Congress party's flag of 1931 even placed a spinning wheel at its centre.

Making khadi starts with cleaning and fluffing raw cotton. The spinner draws the fibres out while the charkha twists them into thread, winding it onto a spindle. Gandhi later used a small folding box charkha that could be carried around like a briefcase.

The hand-spun thread is then woven on a handloom, much like the [[@weaving-saree|looms]] used for sarees. Hand-spun thread is slightly uneven, which gives khadi its texture. The loose weave lets air through, so khadi feels cool in summer and, in thicker weaves, warm in winter.

After independence, the government set up the Khadi and Village Industries Commission to support khadi spinners and weavers, many of them women in villages. Khadi shops, called Khadi Bhandars, still sell cloth, clothes, soap and honey made by village workers.

For decades, the official rules said India's national [[@flags|flag]] should be made of hand-spun khadi. The rules were changed in 2021 to also allow machine-made cloth, a decision some khadi workers were unhappy about. Today many [[@fashion-history|fashion designers]] use khadi for modern clothes, and on Gandhi Jayanti every 2 October, khadi shops often hold big sales.

text: Bullying is when someone keeps hurting another person on purpose, and the person being hurt finds it hard to make it stop. It can be hitting or pushing, name-calling, leaving someone out, spreading rumours, or sending nasty messages online.

If it is happening to you, the most useful step is to tell an adult you trust: a parent, a teacher, a school counsellor or an older relative. If it keeps going, tell another adult, and another. If you see it happening to someone else, there are small, safe things you can do that make a real difference.

st.prompt: Researchers in Canada filmed children at playtime. When a classmate stepped in to stop bullying, what usually happened?

options.t: The bullying often stopped within about ten seconds
The bullying nearly always got worse
The classmate usually got bullied instead

st.reveal: In more than half the cases where a classmate stepped in, the bullying stopped within about ten seconds. Bullies often want an audience, so when the audience turns against them, the fun goes out of it.

d.try: With a friend or family member, think of three short, calm sentences you could say if you saw someone being picked on, such as "Leave it, let's go" or "That's not funny." Practise saying them out loud in an ordinary voice. Having words ready makes it much easier to speak up when it matters.
myth: Bullying is a normal part of growing up, and it makes children tougher.

Studies in many countries link being bullied to worry, poor sleep, headaches and falling marks, and the effects can last for years. It is common, but it is not harmless, and adults are right to take it seriously.

sec.t:
Friends sometimes argue, and people sometimes say mean things once and feel sorry later. Researchers usually call something bullying when three things are true. It is on purpose. It happens again and again. And one side has more power, because they are older, stronger, more popular or part of a group.

That power gap is why "just sort it out yourselves" so rarely works. The person being bullied is not on equal ground. One of the first people to study this carefully was a Norwegian psychologist, Dan Olweus, who began surveying schoolchildren in the 1970s. His work helped schools across the world see bullying as a problem for the whole school, not just two children.

sec.h: If it is happening to you
sec.t:
Bullying is never your fault, whatever the bully says. It can feel embarrassing to tell, but adults who work with children hear about it often. These steps help:

- **Tell someone.** Say what happened, when and where, and who saw it. Adults can do things children cannot, like changing seating or talking to parents. - **Keep a record.** Write down dates. For [[@cyberbullying|cyberbullying]], take screenshots before blocking or reporting. - **Stay near friends** in the places where it tends to happen, like corridors, buses or the lunch queue. - **Try not to hit back.** It is a fair feeling, but it often gets the wrong person into trouble.

Bullying can cause real [[@stress|stress]]: stomach aches, trouble sleeping, not wanting to go to school. Those are signals worth sharing with a parent or doctor too.

{{story:mental-health}}

sec.h: The power of the people watching
sec.t:
When researchers in Toronto filmed playgrounds, they found other children were watching in most bullying episodes. Usually they did nothing, or even laughed. But when someone did step in, the bullying often stopped within about ten seconds.

You don't have to be a hero. You can refuse to laugh, walk away with the person being picked on, say "Come on, let's go," or tell a teacher later. Sitting next to someone who has been left out is a quiet way of standing up for them. All of this comes from [[@empathy|empathy]], the ability to sense how a situation feels from the inside.

In India, the CBSE has asked its schools to set up anti-bullying committees, and colleges have strict rules against ragging, the hazing of new students. In the United States, every state has an anti-bullying law or policy. Schools that do best tend to have clear rules, adults who watch the playground and lunchroom, and children who know exactly whom to tell.

Many schools now train older students to look out for younger ones, and some use a box or an app where children can report bullying without giving their name. Finland's KiVa programme, developed at the University of Turku, is used in schools in many countries.

Plenty of grown-ups were bullied as children, and many of them say the moment that changed things was when one person, a [[@friendship|friend]] or a teacher, simply noticed.

text: The Nobel Peace Prize is a yearly award for the person or group that has done the most to bring nations together, reduce wars or protect people's rights.

It was set up by Alfred Nobel, a Swedish chemist who [[@accident-dynamite|invented dynamite]] and grew very rich. When he died in 1896, his will left most of his money for five prizes. Four are awarded in Sweden. The Peace Prize is chosen by a committee in Norway and handed out in Oslo every 10 December, the day Nobel died.
Winners get a gold medal, a certificate and prize money of around a million US dollars. More than 100 people and about 30 organisations have won it.

Stockholm, like the others

st.reveal: Alfred Nobel wrote in his will that a Norwegian committee should choose the Peace Prize. Nobody knows exactly why. In his time, Sweden and Norway were joined under one king, and Norway's parliament was known for working on peace between countries.

myth: Mahatma Gandhi won the Nobel Peace Prize.

Gandhi was nominated five times, the last in 1948, but never won. After his death, no prize was given that year. The Nobel Committee has since said that leaving him out was one of its biggest mistakes.

sec.t:
Alfred Nobel was born in Stockholm in 1833. He worked with explosives and, in 1867, patented dynamite, which made blasting rock for [[@tunnels|tunnels]], mines and railways much safer and easier. He built factories in many countries and held more than 350 patents.

Dynamite was also used in war, and Nobel's company made weapons. Many people have wondered whether that weighed on him. What we know for sure is what he wrote in his will in 1895. Most of his fortune would pay for prizes in physics, chemistry, medicine, literature and peace.

His family was shocked, and some tried to challenge the will. It took about five years to sort out, which is why the first prizes were only handed out in 1901.

Thousands of people are allowed to nominate, including members of national parliaments, university professors and past winners. Each year the committee receives a few hundred nominations. Its five members, chosen by Norway's parliament, study the list for months and announce the winner in October.

The prize doesn't have to go to a single person. The International Committee of the Red Cross has won it three times, more than anyone else. The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, has won twice.

Some years, the committee gives no prize at all. That happened often during the two world wars, when nobody seemed to deserve it.

Mahatma [[@gandhi|Gandhi]] was nominated five times, but the committee never chose him. In 1948, the year he was killed, no prize was given, and the committee said there was "no suitable living candidate". Decades later, its own historians wrote that leaving [[@gandhi-south-africa|Gandhi]] out was its greatest omission.

Some winners have been controversial. In 1973, two committee members resigned over the prize given to the American official Henry Kissinger, who was involved in the Vietnam War. People argue about other choices too, because peace is hard to measure.

The names of people nominated are kept secret for 50 years. So, today, nobody outside the committee can know who almost won.

text: India's [[@lok-sabha-rajya-sabha|Parliament]] is the group of people who make the country's laws, decide how the government spends money, and keep a close eye on the government. It has two houses. The Lok Sabha, or House of the People, has 543 members elected directly by voters. The Rajya Sabha, or Council of States, speaks for the states and has up to 250 members.
Strictly speaking, the President of India is also part of Parliament, because no bill becomes a [[@laws-made|law]] without the President's signature.

st.prompt: How many members of the Lok Sabha are elected by voters?
st.reveal: India is divided into 543 areas called constituencies, and each one elects one member to the Lok Sabha. The biggest states send the most members. Uttar Pradesh alone sends 80.

d.try: Hold a family Question Hour. One person plays a minister in charge of something at home, like snacks or screen time. Everyone else gets to ask one question, and the minister has to answer properly. Notice how hard it is to dodge a good question.
myth: Members of the Rajya Sabha are elected directly by the people, just like the Lok Sabha.

Most Rajya Sabha members are elected by the MLAs of each state's legislative assembly. The President also nominates 12 members known for work in fields like art, science, literature or social service.

sec.t:
The Lok Sabha is the more powerful house. Every five years, India holds a general election, and whichever party or group of parties wins a majority of Lok Sabha seats forms the government. Its leader becomes Prime Minister. If the government ever loses the support of a majority in the Lok Sabha, it must resign.

The Rajya Sabha never dissolves. Its members serve six-year terms, and about a third of them retire every two years, so the house changes a little at a time. It works like a second pair of eyes, reading bills slowly and suggesting changes. For money bills, such as taxes, it can only make suggestions, and the Lok Sabha has the final word.

A sitting of the Lok Sabha usually begins with Question Hour. Members ask ministers about anything from train accidents to vaccine supplies, and the minister must reply on the record. It is one of the main ways Parliament holds the government to account. The Speaker, an elected member, chairs the Lok Sabha and keeps order. The Vice-President of India chairs the Rajya Sabha.

Parliament usually meets in three sessions a year: the Budget session early in the year, the Monsoon session in July and August, and the Winter session near the end of the year.

For more than 90 years, Parliament met in a round building in [[@delhi|Delhi]] designed by the British architects Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker and finished in 1927. Its outer ring of pillars made it look a bit like a giant wheel. In 2023, Parliament moved into a new triangular building next door. The new Lok Sabha chamber has a peacock theme, India's national bird, and the Rajya Sabha chamber is decorated with [[@lotus|lotus]] designs.

Each state sends Lok Sabha members according to its population, so a large state like Uttar Pradesh sends 80 while [[@sikkim|Sikkim]] sends 1. That is why [[@states-india|India's states]] matter so much at election time. Members speak in many languages, and interpreters translate debates as they happen, so an MP from Kerala can follow a speech made in [[@hindi-language|Hindi]] or Bengali. Compare it with the American system in [[@congress-usa|How does the US Congress work?]], where every state gets the same number of senators.

text: Almost nothing would happen to the planet. When you jump, your legs push Earth away from you, just a tiny bit. All of humanity weighs roughly 400 million tonnes. Earth weighs about 6 thousand billion billion tonnes, or around 15 trillion times more.

So if 8 billion people leapt half a metre in the air at the same second, Earth would shift by less than a thousandth of the width of one atom. Then everybody would land, gravity would pull Earth back, and the score would be even again. The bigger story is what happens if everyone first has to gather in one place to do it.

st.prompt: If all 8 billion people jumped at the same moment, what would happen to Earth?

options.t: It would move by much less than the width of an atom, then move back
It would be knocked slightly out of its orbit
It would start spinning a little faster for ever

st.reveal: Earth is around 15 trillion times heavier than all of humanity. When we push down, it moves a tiny amount, and when we land, it moves back. Overall, nothing changes.

d.try: Stand on a skateboard, or wear socks on a smooth floor, and throw a heavy cushion forwards. You will slide backwards a little. Now think about doing that against something 15 trillion times heavier than everyone you know put together.
myth: If everyone jumped together, Earth would be pushed out of its orbit.
Every push down on Earth is matched by a pull back when you land. Earth also moves around the Sun at about 30 km every second, so a jump is nothing compared with that speed.

sec.t:
Packed shoulder to shoulder, about four people fit in a square metre. Eight billion people would need roughly 2,000 square km. That is about one and a half times the size of Delhi, or about two-thirds the size of the US state of Rhode Island.

The cartoonist Randall Munroe worked through this exact idea in his book *What If?* He put everyone in Rhode Island. With every human squeezed into one patch of land, the jump suddenly becomes something you could measure.

sec.h: Crowds really do shake the ground
sec.t:
We know this because smaller crowds have done it. In 2011, Seattle football fans cheered so wildly after one famous run that a nearby seismometer picked it up. People nicknamed it the "Beast Quake".

In July 2023, [[@taylor-swift|Taylor Swift]] played two concerts in the same stadium. About 70,000 fans dancing and jumping each night produced shaking equal to an earthquake of magnitude 2.3. A seismologist at Western Washington University studied the readings and the "Swift Quake" made news worldwide. Cricket fans at a big IPL final probably make their own small wobbles too, though nobody has measured them.

Munroe pointed out that the jump is the easy part. The hard part is going home. Picture all 8 billion of us standing in one small area with no food, no water and no toilets. There would be nowhere near enough roads, trains, ships or planes to carry everyone back.

Even a city of a crore people struggles when a few lakh pilgrims arrive for one festival. Moving the entire planet's [[@population|population]] would take months, maybe years. Most of the danger would come from the crowd itself, not from Earth.

There is also the timing problem. With people spread across every time zone, "at once" means midnight for some and lunchtime for others. Even counting down together would be hard, because a radio signal takes about a fifteenth of a second to go halfway round the planet.

A single jump lasts less than a second. Earth's mass barely notices. Gravity pulls us all back down at the same rate, whether we weigh 20 kg or 100 kg, as you can see in how [[@gravity-fall|falling objects]] behave.

And here is the oddest twist: Earth moves under your feet every time you jump in the playground, just by an amount far too small to ever detect.

text: Artists use maths all the time, sometimes on purpose and sometimes by instinct. Perspective, which makes a flat painting look deep, is geometry. Symmetry, which gives the Taj Mahal its calm balance, is geometry too. Tile patterns, kolams and quilts are built from shapes that fit together by mathematical rules.

Some artists love maths openly. The Dutch artist [[@maths-art-escher|M. C. Escher]] drew birds that turn into fish and staircases that climb forever. Others use simple rules of thumb, such as dividing a picture into thirds. Today, digital artists use maths in every line of code, and some create art by turning [[@equations|equations]] into pictures.

They stay the same distance apart all the way

st.reveal: Parallel lines going away from the viewer seem to meet at a vanishing point on the horizon. Renaissance artists learned to use this geometry to make flat pictures look deep. Look down a railway track and you can see it for yourself.

d.try: Draw a 5 × 5 grid of dots on paper. Now draw one continuous line that loops around every dot without touching any of them and without lifting your pencil, ending where you began. This is the idea behind many kolam designs. Try it again with a 3 × 3 grid if it's too hard.
myth: The golden ratio was used to design the Parthenon, the Mona Lisa and most great art.

There is little evidence that ancient Greek architects or Leonardo planned their work with the golden ratio. You can find almost any ratio in a building if you choose where to measure. Some later artists did use it on purpose, though.

sec.t:
Before the 1400s, many European paintings looked rather flat. Distant people were not always smaller, and buildings tilted oddly. Then, in Florence, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi worked out the rules of [[@perspective|perspective]]. In 1435, Leon Battista Alberti wrote them down in a book called *On Painting*.

The key idea is the vanishing point. Lines that run straight away from the viewer, like the edges of a road or railway, appear to meet at a single point on the horizon. Objects shrink in size by a regular amount as they get further away. Leonardo da Vinci's *Last Supper* uses perspective so that all the lines of the room lead to Jesus's head at the centre.

In South India, especially Tamil Nadu, many women draw a [[@art-kolam|kolam]] every morning at the doorstep, using rice flour. Many kolams start with a grid of dots called *pulli*. The artist then draws lines that loop around the dots, often in one continuous line that ends where it started.

Mathematicians and computer scientists have studied kolams, because they follow precise rules of symmetry and repetition. Some patterns can be grown step by step, like the instructions in a computer program. Similar patterns turn up in [[@rangoli-symmetry|rangoli]] across India.

Many great buildings use symmetry. The [[@taj-mahal|Taj Mahal]] is almost perfectly mirror-symmetrical, with matching minarets and gardens on either side. Its reflection in the long pool doubles the effect. Indian temples, [[@gothic-cathedrals|Gothic cathedrals]] and the US Capitol in Washington all use symmetry to feel calm and grand.

Mathematicians describe several kinds. Mirror symmetry means one half reflects the other, like a butterfly. Rotational symmetry means a design looks the same after a turn, like a [[@rangoli-art|rangoli]], a wheel or the round rose window of a cathedral. Translation symmetry means a pattern repeats as it slides along, like the border of a saree or a row of block-printed flowers. Artists often mix all three, then break the pattern in one small place to catch your eye.

The golden ratio, about 1.618, is often said to be hidden in great art. Some modern artists and designers have used it on purpose. But many claims are doubtful. Historians have found little evidence that the builders of the Parthenon or Leonardo planned their work with it. Measure a building in enough places and you can find almost any number you want.

What is certain is that artists today have more maths at hand than ever. Computer graphics use geometry to draw every frame of an animated film. [[@fractals|Fractals]], shapes that repeat at smaller and smaller sizes, can be turned into pictures of coastlines, clouds and ferns that look strikingly real.

Children grew up with Tom and Jerry, Scooby-Doo and Swat Kats, and then with Japanese shows like Doraemon, Shin-chan and [[@pokemon|Pokémon]]. In 2008, an Indian-made cartoon, [[@chhota-bheem|Chhota Bheem]], became a hit of its own.

Dubbing writers often change jokes, names and references so they make sense to local viewers, and they must fit the lines to the characters' mouth movements. A good dub is closer to rewriting than to word-for-word translation.

sec.t:
In the 1990s, cable and [[@satellite-tv|satellite TV]] spread across Indian cities. Cartoon Network arrived in the mid-1990s, at first sharing time with a film channel and showing cartoons mostly in English.

Classic American cartoons like Tom and Jerry, The Flintstones and Scooby-Doo became daily viewing. So did newer shows like Dexter's Laboratory, Johnny Bravo and The Powerpuff Girls. Swat Kats, about two cat pilots fighting villains, was a huge favourite with Indian children, and many still ask for it to return.

The big change came with [[@dubbing-subtitles|dubbing]]. Channels began showing cartoons in Hindi, and later in Tamil, Telugu and other languages. Children who did not speak much English could now follow every joke.

Dubbing artists did more than translate. They rewrote jokes, added Indian expressions and gave characters a desi flavour. [[@pop-cartoon-voices|Shin-chan's Hindi voice]] became famous for its cheeky lines. The best dubs felt as if the cartoons had been made in India all along.

In the 2000s, more channels arrived, including Pogo and Hungama. They brought many Japanese cartoons, or [[@manga-anime|anime]]. Doraemon, a blue robot cat from the future with a pocket full of gadgets, became one of the most-watched children's shows in India.

Shin-chan, a naughty five-year-old, was also hugely popular. Some parents complained about his rude behaviour, and in 2008 the show was taken off air for a while, then returned with edits. Pokémon, Beyblade and Dragon Ball also gathered big fan bases.

For years, almost all cartoons on Indian TV came from abroad. Indian [[@animation-studios|animation studios]] mostly did outsourced work for foreign companies. That began to change in 2008, when Chhota Bheem, made by Green Gold Animation in Hyderabad, started on Pogo.

Its village setting, Indian festivals and [[@food-laddoo|laddoo-loving]] hero made it a giant hit. Other Indian shows followed, such as Motu Patlu, based on characters from the comic magazine Lotpot.

Today children watch on phones and streaming apps as much as on TV, and can pick from thousands of shows at any hour. But many adults still remember rushing home to catch one show at one fixed time, with the whole family crowded around one screen.

text: Fashion keeps changing because clothes say something about the people who wear them. When a style becomes common, people who want to stand out move on to something new. Others then copy that, and the cycle starts again.

New inventions, trade and events also push fashion along. A new dye, fabric or machine can make a style cheap enough for everyone. Wars, music, films and now [[@social-media|social media]] can make a look popular almost overnight. Some sociologists think fashion moves in cycles, with old styles returning every few decades, though that is hard to prove.

st.prompt: In the 1940s, skirts in Britain and the USA got shorter and suits lost their trouser turn-ups. Why?

options.t: Cloth was rationed during the Second World War

st.reveal: During the war, governments limited how much fabric could be used for ordinary clothes, so factories cut out extra pleats, cuffs and length. The rules changed what people wore for years.

Designers matter, but fashion also changes because of new materials, prices, weather, wars, music, films and what young people choose to wear. Many styles start on the street and are copied by designers later.
facts: tens of billions of pieces a year

sec.t:
In 1904, the German thinker Georg Simmel suggested that fashion "trickles down". Rich people wear something new to show their status. Others copy it, and the rich move on. In the past, this was easy to see, because fine cloth and dyes were costly.

Today the flow often goes the other way. Styles from skateboarders, musicians and teenagers, such as [[@sneakers|sneakers]] and hoodies, are picked up by designers and sold in expensive shops. Either way, fashion is a balance between fitting in with a group and standing out from it.

During the [[@industrial-revolution|Industrial Revolution]], machines began spinning and weaving cloth far faster than people could by hand. Cotton became cheap. In the 1850s, the [[@sewing-machines|sewing machine]] spread, and factories could make ready-made clothes in standard sizes.

Before this, most people owned only a few outfits, often mended for years. Now, clothes could change with the seasons. Shops published catalogues, and magazines told readers what was "in". Later, cheap synthetic fibres such as nylon and polyester arrived in the 1900s.

Sometimes clothes carry a political message. During India's [[@freedom-struggle|freedom struggle]], Mahatma Gandhi urged Indians to spin and wear [[@khadi|khadi]], handwoven cloth, instead of factory cloth from Britain. Burning foreign cloth and wearing khadi became a way of saying "we want to rule ourselves".

Other events changed fashion too. During the [[@world-war-two|Second World War]], cloth was rationed, so skirts got shorter and suits simpler. In the 1960s, young people in India and the USA wore bell-bottom trousers, bright prints and long hair, partly to show they were different from their parents.

Today, some companies can design a style, make it and put it in shops within a few weeks. This is called fast fashion. It makes clothes cheap, but it also uses huge amounts of water and energy, and many clothes are thrown away after being worn only a few times.

Some people now choose "slow fashion": buying fewer, better clothes, mending them and swapping or buying second-hand. A handloom saree passed from grandmother to granddaughter is slow fashion that has been around for centuries, as [[@weaving-saree|saree weaving]] shows.

text: Gymnasts flip by pushing hard against the floor, a springboard or a bar to launch themselves upwards and set their bodies spinning. Once in the air, nothing can change how much spin they have. But they can change how fast they turn by changing their shape.

Pulling the knees and arms in tight, called a tuck, makes them spin faster. Stretching out slows the spin. To land, a gymnast opens out at the right moment, spots the floor and bends the knees to soak up the force of hitting the ground.

st.prompt: A gymnast doing a somersault wants to spin faster. What should they do?

options.t: Pull their knees and arms in tight to their chest
Stretch their arms and legs out wide
Kick their legs in the air

st.reveal: Tucking in brings the body's mass closer to the centre of the spin, so it spins faster. Opening out slows the spin down, ready for landing. Ice skaters use exactly the same trick.

d.try: Sit on a swivel chair with your arms stretched out, and ask a friend to give you a gentle spin. Then pull your arms in to your chest. You should speed up. Stretch them out again and you slow down. Keep it gentle and stop if you feel dizzy.
myth: Gymnastics is still scored out of a perfect 10.
Since 2006, a score adds a difficulty mark to an execution mark out of 10. Top scores are now often in the 14s and 15s, so a perfect 10 no longer exists.

floor, pommel horse, rings, vault, parallel bars, horizontal bar

sec.t:
Spinning objects carry something physicists call angular [[momentum|momentum]]. Once a gymnast leaves the ground, the total amount stays the same. If they pull their body in closer to the centre of the spin, they have to spin faster to keep the same amount.

This is why a gymnast tucks for a double somersault and opens out to land. [[@gravity-fall|Gravity]] gives them a limited time in the air, often less than a second, so every turn must be squeezed into it. [[@power-cats-landing|Twists]] work in a similar way, using arm movements to tilt the body.

sec.h: From the gymnasium to the Olympics
sec.t:
The word gymnastics comes from the [[@ancient-greece|ancient Greek]] "gymnos", meaning naked, because [[@oddity-ancient-olympics-weird|Greek athletes trained without clothes]] at the gymnasium. Modern gymnastics took shape in [[@germany|Germany]] in the early 1800s. A teacher named Friedrich Ludwig Jahn is credited with inventing the parallel bars and the horizontal bar.

Gymnastics was part of the first modern [[@olympics|Olympics]] in 1896. Women's events joined in 1928. Today women compete on four pieces of apparatus and men on six, each testing different [[@muscles|muscles]]. The balance beam is just 10 cm wide, narrower than a mobile phone is long, and more than a metre off the floor.

At the 1976 Montreal Olympics, 14-year-old Nadia Comăneci of Romania scored the first perfect 10. The scoreboard could only show three digits, so it read 1.00.

In 2006, gymnastics replaced the perfect 10 with an open-ended system. One panel scores difficulty, adding points for harder skills. Another scores execution out of 10, taking points off for mistakes. That rewarded gymnasts who tried harder skills. American [[@simone-biles|Simone Biles]] has so many original moves that several are named after her.

At the 2016 Rio Olympics, Dipa Karmakar of Tripura became the first Indian woman to compete in Olympic gymnastics. She finished fourth in the vault final, performing the Produnova, one of the most dangerous vaults in the sport.

India also has its own gymnastic tradition, mallakhamb, where athletes perform poses and spins on a wooden pole or a hanging rope. It grew in Maharashtra and is now played at India's national games. Like modern [[@skateboarding|skateboarding]], it shows how far balance and practice can take a human body.

text: A movie shows still pictures, called frames, one after another, usually [[@how-cameras-speed|24 every second]].

Shown fast enough, your brain fills in the gaps and sees smooth movement. Each frame is a tiny bit different from the one before: an arm a little higher, a car a little further along. Your brain joins the changes into motion, the same way it tracks a cricket ball or a moving bus.
India's first full-length film, Raja Harishchandra (1913), was made by [[@dadasaheb-phalke|Dadasaheb Phalke]]. India's top film award is named after him.

quiz.prompt: Roughly how many still pictures per second does your brain need before it starts to see smooth movement?

options.t: About 10 to 12
Just 1
About 1,000

quiz.reveal: At around 10 to 12 pictures a second, most people start to see movement rather than a slideshow. Films use 24, which looks smoother. Early silent films often ran at about 16 to 18, which is why old movies can look jerky.

d.try: Make a two-sided spinner, called a thaumatrope. With an adult's help, cut a circle of card, draw a bird on one side and an empty cage on the other, upside down. Tape a pencil to the back, or thread string through two holes, and spin it fast. The bird appears to sit inside the cage.
myth: Movies work because of "persistence of vision", where each picture lingers on the eye until the next one arrives.

Scientists now think this is not the main reason. Your brain sees movement because it actively links small changes between pictures, the same way it notices motion in real life. A lingering image alone would only blur the frames together.
facts: each frame flashed two or three times by the projector

sec.t:
In 1878, Eadweard Muybridge set up 12 cameras in a row to photograph a galloping horse. His pictures proved that, for a moment, all four hooves leave the ground.

The horse ran past the cameras, tripping threads that fired each shutter in turn. Later, Muybridge put the pictures on a spinning glass disc and projected them, so audiences saw the horse gallop. It was one of the first steps towards cinema. Modern [[@cameras-how|cameras]] do the same job far faster.

The Lumière brothers of France held one of the [[@hist-first-film|first paid film shows]] in [[@paris|Paris]] in 1895. Just months later, in July 1896, their films were shown at Watson's Hotel in Bombay. Indians soon started making short films of their own.

Dadasaheb Phalke made Raja Harishchandra after watching a film about the life of Jesus. With no actresses willing to act, a man played the queen. The film was shown in Bombay in 1913 and was a hit. Phalke went on to make many more films about gods and heroes, using clever camera tricks.

Silent films had no fixed speed, and cameras were often cranked by hand at about 16 to 18 frames a second. When sound arrived in the late 1920s, the sound was printed on the film itself, so the speed had to be steady. Studios settled on 24 frames a second, and cinema has mostly kept it ever since.

TV is a little different. In India, TV pictures traditionally ran at 25 frames a second, while in the USA they ran at about 30, because of the different [[@electricity-made|electricity]] supply in each country. A few films, such as *The Hobbit* in 2012, have tried 48 frames a second for extra smoothness, but many viewers said it looked too real, like a TV show.

For about a century, movies were shot on long strips of film. A two-hour movie used kilometres of it. Today, most films are shot and shown digitally, as files of numbers on hard drives. But the idea is the same as Muybridge's horse: still pictures, shown fast, and a brain that turns them into a story. From [[@satyajit-ray|Satyajit Ray]] to the latest cartoon, every film depends on it.

text: Thanksgiving is a national holiday in the United States, held on the fourth Thursday of November. Families gather for a big meal, usually with roast turkey, stuffing, cranberry sauce, mashed [[@potatoes|potatoes]] and pumpkin pie. It is a day for giving thanks, especially for the harvest and for family.

The holiday is often traced to a harvest feast in 1621 at Plymouth, in what is now Massachusetts. English settlers called the Pilgrims shared it with Wampanoag people, who had lived in the area for thousands of years. [[@canada|Canada]] has its own Thanksgiving, on the second Monday of October.

st.prompt: In 1939, President Franklin Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving one week earlier. Why?

options.t: To give shops a longer Christmas shopping season
To avoid snowstorms in late November
To match Canada's Thanksgiving

st.reveal: In 1939, November had five Thursdays, so the last one fell very late. Shop owners asked for more time to sell before Christmas. The change was so unpopular that in 1941 Congress fixed Thanksgiving as the fourth Thursday of November.

myth: The Pilgrims and Native Americans became lasting friends at the first Thanksgiving.
The 1621 meal was a moment of peace between two groups who needed each other. In the decades that followed, war, disease and the loss of land devastated the Wampanoag and other Native nations.

sec.t:
In 1620, a ship called the *[[@pilgrims-mayflower|Mayflower]]* carried about a hundred English settlers across the Atlantic. Many were seeking freedom to worship in their own way. They arrived as winter began, and about half died in the first months.

The Wampanoag, led by Massasoit, had their own reasons to make an alliance. A Patuxet man named Tisquantum, or Squanto, who spoke English, helped the settlers plant corn. In autumn 1621, after their first harvest, the settlers held a celebration. About 90 Wampanoag men joined them, and the feast lasted three days.

For two centuries, different colonies and states held days of thanksgiving at different times. A magazine editor named Sarah Josepha Hale wrote letters for about 17 years asking for one national day.

In 1863, during the [[@us-civil-war|Civil War]], President [[@abraham-lincoln|Abraham Lincoln]] declared a national day of thanksgiving on the last Thursday of November. In 1941, Congress fixed it as the fourth Thursday. That's why it moves between 22 and 28 November, as [[@calendars|calendars]] can explain.

Since 1924, Macy's department store has held a Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City, with [[@made-balloons|giant balloons]] floating between [[@skyscrapers|skyscrapers]]. Professional [[@american-football|American football]] games on Thanksgiving have been a tradition since the 1920s, and millions watch on TV after lunch.

Every year, the President "pardons" a turkey at the [[@white-house|White House]], so it is not eaten. The day after Thanksgiving, called Black Friday, is one of the busiest shopping days of the year. For many families, though, the best part is simpler: relatives who live far apart travel home, and airports and highways are packed for days before the holiday.

For many Native Americans, Thanksgiving recalls the start of great losses. Disease, war and the taking of land devastated [[@native-nations|Native nations]] after the settlers arrived. Since 1970, some Native Americans have gathered at Plymouth on Thanksgiving for a National Day of Mourning.

Many schools now teach both sides of the story. The idea of a harvest festival of thanks is shared by cultures around the world. India has [[@onam-pongal|Pongal and Onam]], Lohri and [[@art-bihu|Bihu]], each celebrating a harvest with its own [[@festival-foods|special food]].

text: The internet reached Indian universities and research labs in the late 1980s, through a network called ERNET that started in 1986. Ordinary people got access on 15 August 1995, India's Independence Day, when the government company VSNL launched a public internet service.

Getting online was slow and costly at first. You needed a computer, a phone line and a modem that screeched as it dialled in. Most people first used the internet in cyber cafés. The real explosion came in the 2010s, with cheap smartphones and very cheap mobile data. By 2025, about 95 crore Indians were online.

On desktop computers at home
At cyber cafés

st.reveal: Cyber cafés mattered in the late 1990s and 2000s, but most Indians went online for the first time on a smartphone. Cheap phones and cheap data from 2016 brought hundreds of millions online.

myth: The internet travels through the air from satellites to your phone.

Your phone talks to a nearby tower by radio, but almost everything after that goes through cables. Most of India's international internet traffic arrives through fibre-optic cables lying on the seabed.

sec.t:
When VSNL opened its service, an account cost thousands of rupees, at a time when many office workers earned only a few thousand a month. Lines were few and often busy. Only a few thousand people signed up in the first months, mostly in big cities like Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai, Kolkata, Bengaluru and Pune.

A dial-up connection used a normal telephone line. The modem turned computer data into sounds and back again. The best modems reached about 56 kilobits a second, and connections were often much slower. Downloading a single song could take several minutes, and if someone picked up the phone, the connection dropped.

Smartphones changed everything. Cheap Android phones arrived around 2010, and 3G and then 4G [[@mobile-networks|mobile networks]] followed. But data was still expensive.

In September 2016, a new company, Reliance Jio, offered free 4G data for several months, and other networks were forced to cut prices. Within a few years, a gigabyte cost around ₹10, and data use jumped. Millions of people who had never owned a computer went online for the first time, usually to watch videos, use WhatsApp and look things up in their own language.

The same year, India launched [[@upi-payments|UPI]], a system that lets people send money from their phones in seconds. Today, a vegetable seller in a small town may have a QR code taped to her cart.

sec.h: Where the internet really comes from
sec.t:
The internet feels invisible, but it runs on cables. More than a dozen [[@undersea-internet|undersea cables]] bring data to India's coasts, many of them landing in Mumbai and Chennai. From there, fibre-optic cables carry it across the country, along railway lines, highways and city streets.

The government's BharatNet project has been laying fibre to connect gram panchayats, the village councils, across rural India. It has made progress, though more slowly than first planned.

Even with 95 crore users in 2025, hundreds of millions of Indians are not online. Many live in villages, are older, or cannot afford a smartphone. Surveys have also found that fewer women than men use the internet, especially in rural areas, though the gap has been shrinking.

Language matters too. In the early years, almost everything online was in English. Now much of what Indians read and watch is in Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, Marathi and other languages. For many new users, the internet is a voice note, a video or a payment, and a keyboard hardly comes into it.

text: The printing press made books cheap and quick to copy. Before it, most books in Europe were copied by hand, letter by letter, often by monks. A single Bible could take a scribe more than a year.

Around 1450, in the German city of Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg put together a system that changed this. He cast small metal letters that could be arranged into pages, inked, printed and then rearranged for the next page. He used an oil-based ink that stuck well to metal and a screw press to push paper down evenly. A small team could now print hundreds of copies of a page in a day.

A loom for weaving cloth

st.reveal: Screw presses had long been used to squeeze grapes and olives. Gutenberg adapted one to press paper firmly and evenly onto inked metal letters, again and again.

myth: Johannes Gutenberg invented printing.

Printing from carved wooden blocks was used in China for centuries before him, and Bi Sheng made movable clay type in China in the 1040s. Gutenberg's achievement was a system of metal type, oil-based ink and a press that made printing fast and cheap in Europe.

sec.t:
Gutenberg was far from the first printer. In China, people printed whole pages from carved wooden blocks more than a thousand years ago. The oldest printed book with a date on it is a Buddhist text called the Diamond Sutra, from 868 CE. It was found in a cave at Dunhuang and is now in the British Library in London.

In the 1040s, a Chinese craftsman named Bi Sheng made movable type out of baked clay. [[@ancient-korea|Korea]] later cast metal type. A Korean Buddhist book called the Jikji, printed in 1377, is the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type. In [[@ancient-china|ancient China]], though, movable type was less handy than in Europe, because Chinese writing uses thousands of different characters. Many Chinese printers stuck with carved blocks.

In Europe, with an [[@words-alphabet-order|alphabet]] of only a few dozen letters, movable type spread fast. By 1500, printing shops were working in more than two hundred towns and cities, and millions of books had been printed.

Cheaper books meant more people learned to read. Scientists could share drawings and results exactly, instead of relying on copies full of copying mistakes. Ideas of the [[@renaissance|Renaissance]] moved quickly between countries. In 1517, Martin Luther's arguments against the Church were printed and spread across [[@germany|Germany]] in weeks, helping to start the Protestant Reformation. Pamphlets, maps and later [[@newspapers|newspapers]] followed. Spelling began to settle down too, because printers wanted the same words to look the same in every copy. Gutenberg himself made little money. He lost control of his workshop to his business partner after a court case over unpaid loans.

sec.h: The press reaches India and America
sec.t:
In 1556, Jesuit missionaries set up India's first printing press in [[@india-wonder-goa-history|Goa]]. For centuries afterwards, printing in [[@scripts-india|Indian scripts]] was slow to develop, partly because those scripts have many joined letters that need extra pieces of type. Tamil was one of the first Indian languages printed in its own script, in the 1570s.

In North America, the first press in the English colonies began work in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1639. A year later it printed the Bay Psalm Book, the first book printed in what became the United States.

text: A camel library is exactly what it sounds like: books carried on camels to people who live far from any town. The most famous one began in 1996 in Garissa, in north-eastern Kenya, near the border with Somalia. Many families there are herders who move with their animals to find water and grass. There are few roads, and a van would get stuck in the sand.
So librarians loaded boxes of books onto camels and walked them out to villages and camps. They set up under a tree, spread out mats, and children chose books to borrow until the camels came back.

st.prompt: Why did Kenya's librarians choose camels instead of a van?

options.t: Vans got stuck on sandy tracks, but camels walk through the bush easily
Camels are cheaper to buy than books
Children were scared of vans

st.reveal: Much of north-eastern Kenya has no proper roads. Camels can walk over sand and thorny scrub, carry heavy loads and go a long time without water, which makes them perfect for the job.

d.try: Start a "travelling library" with friends. Each person puts two books in a bag or box. Every week, pass the bag on to the next person, who takes one book out and adds one back. Keep a list inside the bag of who read what.
myth: Libraries need a building.
A library is a shared collection of books that people can borrow. Around the world, libraries travel on camels, donkeys, horses, boats, buses and bicycles to reach readers who live far away.

started in the 1990s by teacher Luis Soriano
