sec.t:
In Garissa, Kenya's camel library used six camels, in two caravans of three, each led by a handler, with librarians travelling alongside. Books are packed into wooden or metal boxes strapped on each side of a camel's hump. A camel can carry a load heavier than two grown men, walk long distances in heat and go days without drinking.

At each stop, the librarians open the boxes, set out a reading tent or mat and help children pick stories, schoolbooks and picture books. Many of the books are in English and Swahili. The [[@camels|camels]] chew on thorny bushes nearby while readers browse. A camel can drink well over 100 litres of water in a few minutes. Then it can walk for days in the heat without drinking again, which is just what a library on legs needs.

Rain, drought and moving families make the work hard. Books get lost when a family moves on, and dust and sun are tough on paper. Still, for many children in the area, the camel library has been the only place to borrow a book.

{{story:camels}}

Kenya's camels have lots of company. In Colombia, a teacher named Luis Soriano started riding two donkeys, Alfa and Beto, into the hills with books in the 1990s. He called it the *Biblioburro*, "donkey library". In Ethiopia, a donkey-drawn cart library has visited villages around the country.

In Mongolia, a children's author named Jambyn Dashdondog has taken books across the Gobi Desert by camel and other means for years. In Bangladesh, where floods cut off villages every monsoon, boats carry libraries along rivers, and some even double as floating schools.

The USA had its own version. During the Great Depression of the 1930s, many families in the Appalachian mountains of Kentucky lived far from roads, schools or libraries. In 1935, a government programme hired local people, mostly women, to deliver books on horseback and mule.

The pack horse librarians rode up to about 160 km a week, crossing creeks and muddy trails in all weather. They carried books, magazines and scrapbooks of recipes and patterns made by the readers themselves. The project ran until 1943.

Some librarians rode routes so remote that they left books at a central house, and families from further up the hollows walked down to collect them. Readers especially asked for magazines and books that taught practical skills, along with children's picture books. At its peak, the project reached about 100,000 people in rural Kentucky.

Reading changes what a child can learn and do, but books are expensive and heavy, and many places have no shop or library. Moving [[@libraries|libraries]] solve that problem by bringing books to readers instead of the other way round. India has its own versions: library buses in cities, cycle libraries in villages, and volunteers who carry books to tribal hamlets.

All of these follow the same simple idea as the very first libraries: books are worth more when they are shared. The ancient world's most famous collection, in Alexandria, is the starting point for the story of the world's [[@great-libraries|great libraries]].

text: In about 1010 CE, the Chola king Rajaraja I finished a temple to Shiva in his capital, Thanjavur. Its tower, called a *vimana*, rises about 66 m. For centuries it was one of the tallest buildings in India.

The builders used [[@rocks-types|granite]], a stone so hard that steel tools blunt on it. They had no cranes, no engines and no steel girders. What they had were thousands of workers, elephants, ropes, wooden rollers and very clever ideas about stacking stone so that gravity holds it together.

st.prompt: The temple's capstone, the dome-shaped crown on top of the tower, is often said to weigh about how much?

st.reveal: Guides and many books give about 80 tonnes. Some scholars think it may be several stones fitted together rather than one block. Either way, it sits about 60 m above the ground.

n.certNote: The temple's age, builder and size are well recorded. How the huge stones were lifted is less certain, because no plan or account of the building work survives. The famous long ramp is a strong tradition, not a proven fact.

myth: The shadow of Brihadeeswara's tower never falls on the ground at noon.
It does. Anyone can see the tower's shadow on the courtyard on a sunny day. The story is popular, but the Sun obeys the same rules in Thanjavur as everywhere else.
facts: since 1987, as one of the Great Living Chola Temples

sec.t:
The [[@cholas|Cholas]] ruled much of South India, and their ships sailed as far as Southeast Asia. Rajaraja wanted a temple that showed this power. He named it Rajarajeswaram. Today most people call it the Brihadeeswara, or "big lord", temple.

Its walls carry long inscriptions in Tamil. They list gifts of gold, land and cattle. They even name about 400 temple dancers, along with the house and share of land each one received. It is like finding a pay sheet from a thousand years ago.

No granite hills sit next to Thanjavur, which lies in the flat, rich delta of the Kaveri river. Most historians think the stone came from quarries around 50 km away.

Workers probably split blocks by cutting rows of holes and hammering in wedges. Then they dragged them on wooden rollers or sledges, pulled by people and elephants. Some blocks weigh many tonnes, heavier than a loaded autorickshaw.

Guides often say the temple holds more than 1 lakh tonnes of granite. Nobody weighed it, so treat that as a rough figure. Even so, if each sledge carried a few tonnes, that means tens of thousands of trips. Most accounts say the building took only about seven years, so huge crowds of people and animals must have been hauling at once.

{{story:lever-lift}}

The tower is hollow inside for much of its height. It narrows as it climbs, in 13 storeys, like a stepped pyramid. Each layer of stone presses down on the one below and locks it in place. In most places, no mortar was used.

The biggest puzzle is the capstone. It is often said to weigh about 80 tonnes, about as heavy as 13 elephants. A local story says workers built an earth ramp about 6 km long, starting at a village now called Sarapallam, "the scaffold's hollow". The stone was then hauled up the slope. Nobody has found firm proof of the ramp, but it is a sensible guess. Others suggest [[@lever-lift|levers]], wooden scaffolds and slow lifting, a few centimetres at a time.

A huge Nandi, the bull who carries Shiva, sits facing the shrine. It is carved from one stone, about 5 m long. Inside, the linga stands about 3.7 m tall, taller than two grown-ups.

The walls hold carved dancers showing the poses of [[@bharatanatyam|Bharatanatyam]]. Chola painters also covered inner walls with murals, which were hidden under later paint until scholars found them in the 20th century. Underneath a layer from the 1600s, Rajaraja's own painters had been waiting all along, with Shiva, dancers and the king himself.

Unlike many ancient buildings, Brihadeeswara is still a working temple. Prayers have been said there for a thousand years. It has survived earthquakes, wars and centuries of heavy rain.

In 1954, it appeared on India's ₹1,000 note. In 2010, its 1,000th birthday was marked with a special coin. And the same Chola workshops produced something just as surprising in metal: the dancing Shiva statues of [[@bronze-casting|Chola bronze casting]].

text: A [[savanna|savanna]] is a wide grassland dotted with trees, often flat-topped acacias. Kenya's savannas are home to some of the largest groups of wild animals left on Earth: elephants, giraffes, zebras, buffalo, [[@animal-migration-land|wildebeest]], rhinos, and the lions, leopards, cheetahs and [[@wild-hyena|hyenas]] that hunt them.

The most famous patch is the Maasai Mara, in the south-west of Kenya. It joins the [[@serengeti|Serengeti]] across the border in Tanzania. Together they make one huge ecosystem where animals wander freely between the two countries, without passports.

Kenya sits right on the equator, yet it is not one big hot plain. Mount Kenya, at about 5,200 m, has glaciers near its peak. The savanna lies in between, warm all year, with rainy seasons that turn the brown grass green almost overnight.

st.reveal: Wildebeest far outnumber everything else, at well over a million. Hundreds of thousands of zebras and gazelles travel with them. Elephants stay out of it and roam on their own.

d.try: Draw a savanna food chain on a sheet of paper. Start with grass, then add a grazer such as a zebra, then a hunter such as a lion. Add a vulture and a dung beetle at the end, and work out what would happen if you rubbed out one link.
myth: Lions are the "king of the jungle".
Lions hardly ever live in jungle. African lions live on open grassland and in dry woodland, like Kenya's savanna, where they can see prey from far away.
facts: over 1 million wildebeest, plus zebras and gazelles

sec.t:
Not all grazers eat the same thing, which is why so many can share one place. Zebras crop the tall, tough tops of grass. Wildebeest follow and eat the shorter, softer middle. Gazelles nibble what is left near the ground. Giraffes skip the grass entirely and browse acacia leaves from 5 m up, curling a long dark tongue around the thorns.

Then come the clean-up crew. Vultures can strip a carcass in under an hour. Dung beetles roll away animal droppings and bury them, which feeds the soil and helps next year's grass grow. Elephants, by pushing over trees, keep the savanna open instead of letting it turn into forest. Some scientists call them the gardeners of the grassland, and you can read how they [[@elephants-talk|talk to each other]] over long distances.

The Maasai have herded cattle on these grasslands for centuries, and the Maasai Mara is named after them. Cattle mean wealth and food, and many Maasai families still live in a ring of houses inside a thorn fence that keeps out lions at night.

Living close to big wild animals is not easy. Lions sometimes kill cattle, and elephants can flatten a field of maize in one night. Kenya now pays some communities to share their land with wildlife, so that tourists' money reaches the people who live next to the lions.

You may hear guides talk about the "Big Five": lion, leopard, elephant, rhino and Cape buffalo. The name sounds like a list of the most beautiful animals, but it began with hunters. These were the five most dangerous animals to hunt on foot.

Today most visitors carry cameras instead. Kenya banned sport hunting in 1977, and its parks and reserves are now a big part of the country's income. India has its own big cats to protect, and the story of the Asiatic lions of [[@lions-gir|Gir]] shows how a tiny group can be brought back. Kenya's own [[@wangari-maathai|Wangari Maathai]] spent her life showing that trees, soil and people are all part of the same plain.

text: Tamil has been spoken and written without a break for more than 2,000 years. Its oldest poems, known as Sangam literature, were composed roughly 2,000 years ago, and schoolchildren in Tamil Nadu still read some of them today. Its oldest surviving grammar, the *Tolkappiyam*, may be almost as old.

Many ancient languages, such as Latin or ancient Egyptian, survive mainly in books or have changed beyond recognition. Tamil is still the everyday language of about 7 crore people in India, and of millions more in Sri Lanka, Singapore, Malaysia and beyond.
In 2004, the Government of India named Tamil its first "classical language", a title for languages with a very long, independent literary tradition.

sec.t:
Tamil belongs to the Dravidian family, along with Telugu, Kannada and [[@malayalam|Malayalam]]. These languages are not descended from [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]], which belongs to a different family, Indo-European. Over the centuries the two families have borrowed many words from each other, but their grammar and everyday core words are separate.

Tamil builds words by sticking pieces together, one after another. *Veedu* means house, and *veettukku* means "to the house". Add more pieces and a single long word can say what English needs a whole phrase for. Linguists call this agglutination, from a Latin word meaning "to glue".

The oldest Tamil writing is in a script called Tamil-Brahmi, carved in caves and scratched on pottery. Many inscriptions date from at least the 2nd century BCE. At Keezhadi, near Madurai, archaeologists have found broken pots marked with Tamil-Brahmi letters. The Tamil Nadu [[@archaeology|archaeology]] department has argued that some are even older than that. Other scholars want more tests before agreeing.

Tamil-Brahmi words have also turned up far from home, on pottery found at Berenike, an ancient port on the Red Sea coast of Egypt. Tamil merchants traded pepper and gems [[@ocean-currents|across the ocean]], long before the [[@cholas|Chola]] kings sent their ships to Southeast Asia.

A living language keeps changing, and Tamil is no exception. Spoken Tamil differs quite a lot from the formal written style, so children learn both. Chennai Tamil, Madurai Tamil and Sri Lankan Tamil each sound different. Tamil films, songs and social media spread new slang every year.

Tamil has given a few words to English too. *Catamaran* comes from *kattumaram*, "tied logs", a kind of boat still used by fishing families along the coast near [[@chennai|Chennai]]. In Singapore, Tamil is one of four official languages, printed on signs beside English, Malay and Chinese. Its oldest poems and its newest [[@film-songs|film songs]] are written with the same letters.

text: Most bread rises because of [[yeast|yeast]], a living fungus made of single cells far too small to see. When you mix yeast into dough, it wakes up and feeds on sugars in the flour. As it feeds, it gives off bubbles of carbon dioxide, the same gas you breathe out.

Those bubbles would simply escape if it weren't for [[gluten|gluten]]. When wheat flour is mixed with water and kneaded, two proteins link up into a stretchy net. The net traps the gas like millions of tiny balloons, and the dough swells. In the oven, the heat makes the bubbles grow bigger, then sets the dough firm around them.

st.prompt: Yeast makes two things as it feeds on dough. One is carbon dioxide gas. What is the other?

options.t: A little alcohol, which mostly escapes in the oven
Extra flour
Salt

st.reveal: Yeast turns sugar into carbon dioxide and a small amount of alcohol. The gas puffs up the dough, and the oven's heat drives off almost all the alcohol, leaving behind some of the warm smell of baking bread.

d.try: Put a teaspoon of dried yeast and a teaspoon of sugar into a small bottle with half a cup of warm (not hot) water. Stretch a balloon over the mouth and wait 30 minutes in a warm spot. The balloon slowly stands up, blown up by gas breathed out by the yeast.

Yeast is alive. Each grain of dried yeast holds sleeping single-celled fungi that wake up in warm water and start feeding. Baking soda is a chemical that makes gas through a reaction, with nothing living involved.

sec.t:
Bakers' yeast is a type of fungus, a distant cousin of [[@mushrooms|mushrooms]]. A single teaspoon of dried yeast holds billions of cells. In warm, wet dough, each cell eats sugar and buds off a new cell every couple of hours.

Flour doesn't contain much sugar at first. It's mostly starch. Natural [[enzyme|enzymes]] in the flour slowly snip the starch into sugars, feeding the yeast. Along with gas, yeast makes a small amount of alcohol and dozens of flavour chemicals. That's why dough left to rise slowly overnight tastes richer.

In a hot oven, bread gets one last burst of growth that bakers call "oven spring". The gas in every bubble expands in the heat, and the yeast works frantically for a few minutes. At about 60 °C the yeast dies. Then the starch and proteins set, locking the bubbles in place.

The outside dries and browns into a crust, as sugars and proteins react to make new colours and smells. The holes you see in a slice of bread are the frozen ghosts of those gas bubbles.

Not every fluffy food uses yeast. Baking soda and baking powder are chemical raising agents. When they meet something acidic, like curd, lemon juice or buttermilk, or get hot, they release carbon dioxide straight away, with no waiting. That's why cake batter, dhokla and soda bread can go into the oven or steamer almost as soon as they're mixed.

Steam can do the job too. Puris swell into golden balloons in hot oil, as water inside the dough suddenly boils.

In 2018, scientists studying an ancient fireplace in Jordan found charred bread crumbs about 14,400 years old. They were flatbreads made from wild grains, baked thousands of years before anyone farmed wheat.

Nobody knows who first made bread rise, but Egyptian bakers were doing it thousands of years ago. Wild yeast floats in the air, so dough left out would have started to bubble on its own. Sourdough still works this way, using wild yeast and helpful bacteria. In the 1850s and 1860s the French scientist Louis Pasteur showed that [[@fermentation|fermentation]] is caused by living things.

In India, soft breads like pav arrived with Portuguese bakers in Goa. But the strangest part? South India's dosa and idli batter rises overnight with no added yeast at all, puffed up by wild microbes in the rice and [[@dosa-idli|urad dal]].

text: Vanilla is the seed pod of an orchid, and it is one of the hardest crops on Earth to grow. Each flower opens for only one day and must be pollinated by hand. Then the green pod takes about nine months to ripen and several more months to dry and "cure" before it smells of vanilla at all.

So every bean has been touched by people many times over about a year. Most of the world's vanilla comes from one place, the island of [[@madagascar|Madagascar]], so a single bad storm can send prices flying. That is why vanilla is often called the second most expensive spice, after [[@saffron|saffron]].

sec.t:
In 1841, on the French island of Réunion in the Indian Ocean, an enslaved 12-year-old named Edmond Albius found a way. Using a thin stick and his thumb, he lifted a small flap inside the flower and pressed the male and female parts together. It took a few seconds.

His method spread to Madagascar, Indonesia, India and beyond, and it is still how almost all vanilla is pollinated today. Albius was freed when slavery ended on the island in 1848, but he never became rich from his discovery. Today there is a statue of him on Réunion.

A fresh green vanilla pod has almost no smell. The flavour comes from curing. Farmers dip the pods in hot water, wrap them in blankets to "sweat", then lay them in the sun each day and wrap them up again each night. This goes on for weeks. Then they dry slowly for months.

During curing, the pods turn dark brown and wrinkly, and a chemical called vanillin forms inside. Good beans may even grow tiny white crystals of vanillin on their skin. One kilogram of cured beans needs about five to six kilograms of green pods.

Because so much vanilla comes from one island, prices jump and crash. After a cyclone hit Madagascar in 2017 and harvests fell, cured beans sold for around 500 to 600 US dollars a kilogram, more than silver at the time. High prices tempted thieves, and some farmers branded their beans with codes, like dabba marks, so stolen ones could be traced. Since then, prices have fallen a long way, which is hard on the farmers too, a pattern explained by [[@supply-demand|supply and demand]].

India grows some vanilla too, mainly in Kerala and Karnataka. Farmers there rushed into it in the early 2000s when prices were high, then many gave up when prices fell.

Real beans could never meet the world's demand. So most "vanilla" flavour, in biscuits, cakes and [[@ice-cream|ice cream]], is vanillin made in factories. It can be made from substances in wood pulp, from clove oil or from chemicals made from oil. It tastes close, but real vanilla has hundreds of other flavour chemicals that the factory version lacks.

And here's the oddest twist: the "plain" flavour of ice cream is the one that took the most work to grow. It shares an ancient story with the Aztec drink that became [[@chocolate-world|chocolate]].

text: Yes. About 2 billion people around the world eat insects as a normal part of their diet, according to the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization. More than 1,900 kinds of insects are eaten, especially beetles, caterpillars, bees, wasps, ants, grasshoppers and crickets.

In many parts of Asia, Africa and Latin America, insects are snacks, side dishes or treats. In India, people in forest and tribal areas of central and eastern India, and in the Northeast, have long eaten certain insects. In the US and Europe, most people find the idea strange. Yet many of them eat insect products every day without knowing, in food colours, sweet coatings and honey.

People have eaten insects for thousands of years, and about 2 billion people still do. What's new is that some Western countries have started selling insect foods in shops.

sec.t:
In the Similipal forests of Odisha, people collect red weaver ants and their eggs from leafy nests in trees. They grind them with salt, ginger, garlic and chilli into a sharp, sour chutney called kai chutney. In January 2024 it was given a Geographical Indication tag, a label that protects foods linked to a particular place.

People in Bastar, in Chhattisgarh, make a similar chutney called chaprah. The ants taste sour because they contain formic acid, a natural acid that gives them a bite. [[@ants-world|Weaver ants]] are the same species famous for stitching leaves together with silk.

In Thailand, fried crickets and grasshoppers are a popular street snack. In [[@mexico|Mexico]], especially Oaxaca, toasted grasshoppers called chapulines are eaten with lime and chilli, often in tacos. In parts of Africa, mopane worms, which are caterpillars, are dried and stewed. In Japan, grasshoppers simmered in soy sauce and sugar are a traditional dish.

In 2021, the European Union approved dried mealworms as a food. Since then, insect flour, burgers and snacks have appeared in some European shops.

Insects are packed with [[@food-nutrients|protein]], and many also have healthy fats, iron and zinc. They are also efficient. The FAO reports that crickets need much less feed than cattle to make the same amount of protein. They use far less water and land too, and give off fewer greenhouse gases.

That is why some scientists think insects could help feed a growing world population. Insect farms already raise insects to feed [[@chickens|chickens]] and fish.

Many people eat insect products without noticing. Carmine, a red colouring made from crushed cochineal bugs, colours some sweets, drinks and yogurts. Shellac, a shiny coating on some sweets and tablets, comes from a resin made by the lac insect. India produces much of the world's lac, much of it from Jharkhand.

[[@honey|Honey]] isn't an insect, of course, but bees make it. And the US Food and Drug Administration accepts that a few tiny insect fragments end up in foods like chocolate and flour, because it's impossible to remove every single one. They're harmless.

People who are allergic to prawns or crabs may also react to insects, because they share similar proteins. Wild insects can carry pesticides, so people who eat them choose them carefully. Eating insects is a food choice like any other: normal in some homes, unthinkable in others, and slowly changing.
